claims.claim: Among adults aged 66 or over with high blood pressure in Ontario, those newly given a calcium channel blocker were more often given a loop diuretic within 90 days than those newly given an ACE inhibitor or ARB or an unrelated drug (1.4% vs 0.7% and 0.5%).
claims.supporting_passage: "The cohort included 41 086 older adults (≥66 years) with hypertension who were newly dispensed a CCB, 66 494 individuals who were newly dispensed another antihypertensive medication, and 231 439 individuals who were newly dispensed an unrelated medication. At index (ie, the dispensing date), the mean (SD) age was 74.5 (6.9) years, and 191 685 (56.5%) were women. Individuals who were newly dispensed a CCB had a higher cumulative incidence at 90 days of being dispensed a loop diuretic than individuals in both control groups (1.4% vs 0.7% and 0.5%, P < .001)."
claims.pico_timeframe: Community-dwelling adults 66+ with hypertension, Ontario 2011 to 2016 / newly dispensed CCB / newly dispensed ACE inhibitor or ARB, or unrelated drug / dispensing of a loop diuretic / 90 days (and up to 1 year)
claims.safe_wording: In Ontario, among people aged 66 or over with high blood pressure, about 14 in every 1,000 people started on a calcium channel blocker such as amlodipine were given a loop diuretic (a strong water tablet such as furosemide) within 3 months. The figure was about 7 in 1,000 for people started on a different blood pressure tablet, and 5 in 1,000 for people started on an unrelated medicine.
claims.qualifications: Dispensing data: shows who was given a diuretic, not whether swelling was the reason. The gap (about 7 extra per 1,000 compared with other blood pressure tablets) is the best estimate of the cascade; it is small per person but large across a population. Association, not proof that each case was a cascade.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: A US claims study (Vouri 2019) found a similar signal (see C06-18-i). No study found that contradicts the direction.

claims.claim: A prescribing cascade is when a side effect of one drug is taken for a new condition and a second drug is prescribed to treat it; the term was described by Rochon and Gurwitz in the BMJ in 1997.
claims.supporting_passage: McCarthy 2022: "Prescribing cascades occur when a drug is prescribed to manage side effects of another drug, typically when a side effect is misinterpreted as a new condition." Savage 2020: "A prescribing cascade occurs when the edema is misinterpreted as a new medical condition and a diuretic is subsequently prescribed to treat the edema." Rochon 1997 record title: "Optimising drug treatment for elderly people: the prescribing cascade."

claims.pico_timeframe: Definition
claims.safe_wording: A prescribing cascade is when a side effect of one medicine is mistaken for a new illness, and a second medicine is started to treat it.
claims.qualifications: Attribute the term to Rochon and Gurwitz (BMJ 1997) only by citation; no text from that article was read.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: ThinkCascades authors note that some cascades are intentional and appropriate (e.g., NSAID plus stomach protection), so not every drug added for a side effect is an error.

claims.claim: Ankle swelling is a common, dose-related side effect of calcium channel blockers of the amlodipine type.
claims.supporting_passage: Makani 2011: "One hundred and six studies with 99 469 participants, mean age 56 ± 6 years, satisfied our inclusion criteria and were included in this analysis. The weighted incidence of peripheral edema was significantly higher in the CCBs group when compared with controls/placebo (10.7 vs. 3.2%, P < 0.0001). Similarly, the withdrawal rate due to edema was higher in patients on CCBs compared with control/placebo (2.1 vs. 0.5%, P < 0.0001). Both the incidence of edema and patient withdrawal rate due to edema increased with the duration of therapy with CCBs reaching 24 and 5%, respectively, after 6 months. ... Incidence of peripheral edema in patients on DHPs was 12.3% compared with 3.1% with non-DHPs (P < 0.0001). candidates.reason: All essential claims supported: Savage 2020 absolute and relative figures (1.4% vs 0.7% vs 0.5% at 90 days; persisted to 1 year and in amlodipine-only subgroup), the definition of a prescribing cascade (McCarthy 2022, Savage 2020), CCB oedema being common and dose-related (Makani 2011), alternatives (lower dose, switch, add ACE inhibitor/ARB; Woodford 2020 says switching is best and the diuretic is justified only when that fails), and downstream harms after a loop diuretic is added (Growdon 2025, qualified: gabapentinoid cascade). Two lead claims are not supported and must not be used: that CCB oedema 'responds poorly to diuretics' (not found), and that ThinkCascades lists this cascade (table not rendered). The draft opening line ('a water tablet is a poor treatment for it') must be reworded to 'is a side effect of the first drug, and the first step is to review that drug'. Label the 'possible third drug' step 'Illustrative example'. Give absolute figures first, as the judge asked.

The triple-combination finding, the first-30-days peak and the absolute context are supported (Lapi 2013 full text; Dreischulte 2015). But the candidate's claim that double combinations were 'not associated' is contradicted by a Scottish study with a more sensitive definition (Dreischulte 2015: similar relative rise with a diuretic alone or an ACE inhibitor/ARB alone). The UK guidance claim (BNF/NICE CKS) and 'paracetamol for most people' could not be sourced. Both Lapi and Dreischulte measured prescribed NSAIDs, not shop-bought ibuprofen.
candidates.revised_angle: If you take a water tablet or a blood pressure tablet such as ramipril or losartan, and especially if you take both, ask a pharmacist before buying ibuprofen or naproxen. Two UK studies link anti-inflammatories taken with these medicines to sudden kidney injury; risk is highest with all three, in the first month, in people over 75 and in people with weaker kidneys. Give the absolute context (for example, about 1 extra kidney injury per 158 people taking an anti-inflammatory for a year alongside both medicines; hospital admission for kidney injury is uncommon). Do not imply one of the medicines alone makes ibuprofen safe, and do not name paracetamol or cite BNF/NICE unless sourced.

candidates.reason: All essential claims supported from the NEJM abstract and full-text excerpts: design (33 of 34 Tayside practices, education plus informatics plus payment to review), nine named measures and the option to record that a prescription is appropriate, primary outcome 3.7% to 2.2% (adjusted OR 0.63), secondary admission outcomes (GI bleeding 55.7 to 37.0, heart failure 707.7 to 513.5 per 10,000 person-years; AKI 101.9 and 86.0, not significant), and the post hoc finding that the reduction was sustained 48 weeks after incentives ceased (2.0%, 560 of 28,616). Admission results are secondary, before-and-during comparisons, and the authors say the intervention 'may have improved clinical outcomes'. Effects varied widely between practices. A 2025 UK trial of a broad polypharmacy review with similar supports (IMPPP) was null; contrasting the two to argue for focus is judgement and must be marked as such.

Lipska 2015 figures are supported but show potential overtreatment, not measured low blood sugars, in US data from 2001 to 2010. No opened source measured hypoglycaemia frequency in frail people with a low HbA1c, so 'a good HbA1c comes with frequent low blood sugars' is stronger than the evidence. Munshi 2011 shows low sugars are common and mostly unnoticed even when HbA1c is high, so HbA1c does not reveal them either way. UK support found: Hambling 2017 (Norfolk: about 3 in 10 people 70+ on sulfonylurea or insulin had HbA1c below 53 mmol/mol, as common in CKD and dementia) and Strain 2018 (usual targets too tight in frailty). Deprescribing recommendation supported by Farrell 2017. Hypoglycaemia linked with falls and fractures (association; Mattishent 2021). ADA Standards could not be opened. Tight control has benefits (Crabtree 2022), which the post should acknowledge.
candidates.revised_angle: For a frail older person taking insulin or a gliclazide-type tablet, a low HbA1c can be a sign of more treatment than they need: in UK and US studies, low HbA1c on these drugs was as common in people in poor health, with kidney disease or with dementia as in healthier people. HbA1c does not show whether low blood sugars are happening, and low sugars are linked with falls and fractures. UK consensus says usual targets are too tight in frailty, and a deprescribing guideline recommends reducing drugs that cause low sugars in people at risk. Question for families: 'Has she had any low sugars, and does she still need this dose?'

candidates.reason: Reserve. The MHRA 2019 advice could only be found as a search-engine extract (not enough for an essential claim), and the mechanism claim (1.73 m2 normalisation, muscle mass) was not found in an opened source. Published studies support that DOAC trials dosed by Cockcroft-Gault (MacCallum 2013, Chan 2022) and that eGFR tends to overestimate kidney function versus Cockcroft-Gault, especially over 75 and under 50 kg (Chan 2022), with 14.9% of people 80+ in east London misclassified as eligible for dabigatran (MacCallum 2013). But a Berlin cohort (median age 87) found outcomes did not differ by equation (Villain 2023), so claims of harm must be hedged.
candidates.revised_angle: Teaching round: DOAC doses were tested using Cockcroft-Gault creatinine clearance, and in people over 75 with low body weight the lab eGFR often reads higher, which can put them in a higher dose band. Calculate creatinine clearance with the person's weight when dosing a DOAC in a small, very old person. Name the conflicting Berlin result and say outcome evidence is mixed. Use the MHRA advice only if an opened copy is found.
